title: Exploring Palmer Penguins using R
Exploring Palmer Penguins using R
text:
Body mass distribution by species

penguins |>
  drop_na(species, body_mass_g) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = species, y = body_mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    x = "Species",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    title = "Penguin Body Mass by Species"
  )







Figure 1: Distribution of body mass for each penguin species.





The boxplot shows that Gentoo penguins generally have a higher body mass than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.

title: Exploring Palmer Penguins using R
text:
Flipper length and body mass
Next, I explored whether penguins with longer flippers also tend to have greater body mass.

penguins |>
  drop_na(flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, species) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = flipper_length_mm,
      y = body_mass_g,
      color = species
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    x = "Flipper length (mm)",
    y = "Body mass (g)",
    color = "Species",
    title = "Flipper Length vs Body Mass"
  )







Figure 2: Relationship between flipper length and body mass by species.





The scatter plot shows a positive relationship between flipper length and body mass. Gentoo penguins tend to have both longer flippers and higher body mass than Adelie and Chinstrap penguins.

title: Exploring Palmer Penguins using R
text:
Average flipper length by species
I also calculated the average flipper length for each species.

penguins |>
  drop_na(species, flipper_length_mm) |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(
    mean_flipper_length = mean(flipper_length_mm),
    median_flipper_length = median(flipper_length_mm),
    n = n()
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 4
  species   mean_flipper_length median_flipper_length     n
  <fct>                   <dbl>                 <dbl> <int>
1 Adelie                   190.                   190   151
2 Chinstrap                196.                   196    68
3 Gentoo                   217.                   216   123


Gentoo penguins have the largest average flipper length, while Adelie penguins generally have the shortest flippers.

iris = load_iris(as_frame=True)
df = iris.frame

df["species"] = df["target"].map(
    dict(enumerate(iris.target_names))

The average measurements differ across the three species. Setosa flowers have substantially shorter and narrower petals, while Virginica flowers generally have the largest petal measurements.

title: Exploring the Iris Dataset using Python
text:
Petal length distribution by species

df.boxplot(
    column="petal length (cm)",
    by="species"
)

plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Petal length (cm)")
plt.title("Petal Length by Species")
plt.suptitle("")
plt.show()







Figure 1: Distribution of petal length for each Iris species.





The box plot shows clear differences in petal length among the three species. Setosa has much shorter petals, while Virginica generally has the longest petals.

title: Exploring the Iris Dataset using Python
text:
Correlation between flower measurements
Next, I examined how strongly the four numerical flower measurements are related to one another.

measurement_columns = [
    "sepal length (cm)",
    "sepal width (cm)",
    "petal length (cm)",
    "petal width (cm)"
]

correlations = df[measurement_columns].corr()

title: Exploring the Iris Dataset using Python
text:
Number of flowers by species
Finally, I checked whether all three species have the same number of observations in the dataset.

species_counts = df["species"].value_counts().sort_index()

species_counts.plot(kind="bar")

plt.xlabel("Species")
plt.ylabel("Number of observations")
plt.title("Number of Flowers by Species")
plt.xticks(rotation=0)
plt.show()







Figure 2: Number of Iris observations for each species.





The bar chart shows that the dataset is balanced: each of the three Iris species has the same number of observations.
